briefing:
The headline Daily Airfare Price Index (APIx) rose to 107.12, representing a 7.12% overall price increase across domestic trunk corridors relative to the base period baseline. Aggregate market dynamics reflect broad-based upward fare pressure, with all three weighted routes demonstrating positive yield growth. The overall movement was primarily led by the Calcutta – Bombay corridor, which recorded the highest inflation with a route-level APIx of 111.60 (+11.60% change from base). The Delhi – Bengaluru corridor followed with a route-level APIx of 106.45 (+6.45%), while the highest-weighted route, Delhi – Bombay (0.40 weight), displayed a more moderate price expansion, reaching a route APIx of 104.28 (+4.28%).

Upward index momentum was heavily driven by intermediate and short-term booking windows, specifically the T+15 and T+30 horizons, which carry a combined 50% weight in the macro index methodology. Granular route details show that Calcutta – Bombay was the critical driver of systemic inflation, where the T+15 median price surged by 35.78% to ₹12,692.5 (up from ₹9,348) and T+1 spot fares expanded by 23.57% to ₹11,843. On the Delhi – Bengaluru route, intermediate windows also experienced significant tightening, with T+30 and T+15 target median prices rising by 12.54% (to ₹9,936) and 9.37% (to ₹10,156) respectively. Conversely, Delhi – Bombay exhibited a stable, low-volatility price trajectory, characterized by a steady 8.69% uptick in T+1 fares (₹7,097.5) and minor upward adjustments ranging between 2.46% and 5.01% across longer lead-time windows.

Micro-level scrape analytics highlight notable fare dispersion across carrier business models and departure infrastructure. The emergence of satellite regional infrastructure created key pricing variances; for example, at the T+7 window on Delhi – Bombay, non-stop flights departing from Jewar (DXN) operated by Akasa Air provided an entry floor of ₹4,860, offering a distinct price relief against standard Indira Gandhi International (DEL) non-stop flights anchored around ₹6,530. Low-cost carriers like Air India Express and SpiceJet consistently anchored the absolute market price floors via 1-stop routes—such as ₹6,245 fares on Delhi – Bombay at T+15 and T+30—whereas legacy non-stop carriers maintained higher median fare levels above ₹6,800. A prominent corridor anomaly appeared on Calcutta – Bombay at the T+45 lead time, where median prices contracted sharply by 24.30% to ₹9,776.5 (down from ₹12,915 baseline), driven by competitive advance booking fares such as SpiceJet’s ₹8,078 non-stop listing.

From a monetary policy and macroeconomic perspective, the elevated airfares across key trunk routes suggest near-term upward pressure on the transport and communication sub-index of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Although short-to-medium horizon price hardening reflects robust passenger demand, the operational integration of secondary airport hubs (such as Jewar and Navi Mumbai) demonstrates early potential to de-escalate capacity bottlenecks over longer lead times. Policymakers should maintain a cautious outlook on aviation services inflation pass-through into core CPI, while closely monitoring high-frequency T+15 and T+7 dynamic booking volatility as a key indicator of underlying domestic consumption resilience.
